doc.title: Barry Kernfeld interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 16, 2020

title: Current jazz, unusual meters and players as robots
summary: They discuss young players' time feel, the fad for playing in any meter, and technique valued over melody in jazz education.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Okay. Well you can go get another drink now at the cocktail party. You deserve it, that was a nice response. I can’t say that I’m a constant listener to current jazz but what I’ve heard of it, something you said about the conventions of it and what we expect and it seems that they — younger players are approaching the time in a different way now. I listen to the bass players and the drummers and a lot — they’re not playing the time, they’re playing against the time. And it’s very creative. It’s hard for me to latch on to I guess. I guess I’m a guy who needs a groove.
Yeah I’m sorry, I don’t actually know what that means or who you have in mind?
Well for one thing it was the San Francisco Jazz Collective that — very accomplished, and perhaps my ears aren’t just modern enough for what they’re doing.

No there’s so many different things happening it’s really hard to say. There’s a huge infatuation with unusual meter. That’s like almost — so as jazz education, you know, formulated itself as a component of universities this idea of playing in all keys became popular. You know can you do “Donna Lee” in every key? And I think that has now morphed into can you do “Donna Lee” in any meter? So that’s a technical thing that is of just about zero interest to me. I don’t care about that. But there are so many different things going on worldwide in jazz. It’s impossible to make any kind of generalization along those lines. There’s fantastically creative players and there’s robots and everything in between in many, many different styles.

It’s just something that got fostered as a component of jazz coming into the university and people focusing obsessively on pitch/scale relationships — you get this chord you play these notes. And on people focusing on technique rather than having technique be subsumed to making melody. Making melody should be the number one consideration. Technique should be at the service of it. And that’s just — I mean so what — there’s — I’m sure that’s true in music for a very long time in many different disciplines. You know it’s just that it’s all more visible now because we have such efficient communications.
